Once more unto the breach. This is King Henry V's rallying cry to his soldiers as they assault the breach in the walls of Harfleur, demanding they harden their resolve and channel their warrior spirit.

Henry delivers this speech in Act III as his army prepares its frontal assault on the French fortress. He opens with the rallying cry: once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more. The phrase echoes the relentless cycle of combat and the will to overcome fear. Henry commands his soldiers to steel their faces, to imitate the action of the tiger, and to summon animal fury and courage. He frames manhood itself as contingent on the willingness to fight. "Now is it time to stir your blood in your veins," he declares.

What distinguishes this speech is how explicitly it demands violence. Henry contrasts the brutality required in war with the civility of peacetime, suggesting that soldiers must temporarily abandon their humanity to succeed. Unlike his later Saint Crispin's Day speech, this one emphasizes action over philosophy, the immediate demand for combat courage rather than transcendent vision. The speech is fundamentally about transformation—turning common men into instruments of war and glory through sheer force of will and rhetoric.
